competitors.name: Hudson Rock (Cavalier, infostealers.com, CavalierGPT)
competitors.what_they_do: Infostealer intelligence. Sells compromised-employee and compromised-domain data and publishes infostealer research. The site fetch was thin, so I could not confirm a specific AI-session-exposure product. It is the most likely source of the '358 of 482' style statistics and the most likely data supplier, or a fast follower that adds an AI-exposure report.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Not verified. The fetched pages showed no funding figures.

competitors.name: SpyCloud
competitors.what_they_do: Identity threat protection: infostealer and breach recapture, session-hijack detection, and 'Identity Guardians' session remediation. Its blog covers session theft generally, and I found no AI-chat-specific content. It covers the detection and revocation half of the idea, not the content-exposure half.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Established, venture-backed. Figures not verified in fetch.

competitors.name: Flare
competitors.what_they_do: Threat exposure management with 101+ blog posts on infostealer logs. It detects stolen credentials and sessions. I found no AI-chat-history impact assessment.

competitors.name: Constella Intelligence
competitors.what_they_do: Says it processed 51.7M infostealer packages in 2025 and holds 'the world's largest breach and infostealer data lake'. It sells to law-enforcement and investigations teams. It could resell the raw feed or add victim identification, but I found no AI-content analysis.

competitors.name: Group-IB (Threat Intelligence)
competitors.what_they_do: Published the 2023 finding of 101,134 stealer-infected devices with saved ChatGPT credentials (June 2022 to May 2023). It recommends password changes and 2FA and sells a threat-intel platform. It proves the exposure exists, but it does not assess content.

competitors.name: Varonis (AI Security, MDDR, Concierge)
competitors.what_they_do: Data security platform that markets protection against 'sensitive data exposure via AI copilots like Microsoft 365 Copilot, ChatGPT Enterprise...'. It classifies AI-generated content, detects compromised AI users, and offers managed data detection and response. Its incident-response page shows no mention of breach-notification scoping for AI chats or of a law-firm or insurer channel. It is the incumbent most likely to add this as a feature.

competitors.name: Cyera (AI Prompt Security, DataWatcher, Incident Materiality Assessment)
competitors.what_they_do: AI-native data classification (claims 95%+ precision) with an 'AI Prompt Security' solution. DataWatcher managed services include 'expert-led data breach response support' and an 'Incident Materiality Assessment'. This is the closest adjacent match to the deliverable (materiality and notification scoping), but it targets the customer's own data stores and I found nothing on stolen-session AI transcripts.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Venture-backed, and the homepage says it recently acquired Oasis. Funding figures not verified.

competitors.name: Harmonic Security
competitors.what_they_do: Collects and classifies prompts sent to ChatGPT and similar tools at the browser, desktop and API layers, with real-time block, warn and log controls and GDPR-oriented logging. It is a prevention and governance tool and does not appear to offer post-incident forensic scoping. It does create a prompt archive that could be the data source for an assessment.

competitors.name: Cyberhaven (Linea AI Analyst Agent)
competitors.what_they_do: Data lineage and DLP that tracks data flowing into generative AI tools and runs AI-driven investigations with incident scoping. It answers 'what did our people paste into ChatGPT'. It does not answer 'what could a stolen session have read'.

competitors.name: Reco
competitors.what_they_do: SaaS and AI-agent security. Shadow-AI discovery covers 260+ apps with OpenAI and Claude integrations, plus threat detection and auto-remediation. It is an OpenAI Select Partner.
competitors.scale_or_funding: $85M total raised, including a $30M Series B (per its own site).

competitors.name: Microsoft Purview (Audit for Copilot and AI applications)
competitors.what_they_do: Audit logs of Copilot and third-party AI app interactions (AIAppInteraction, ConnectedAIAppInteraction), with sensitivity-label references and DLP evaluation. Non-Microsoft AI audit is pay-as-you-go with 180-day retention. It is the platform-vendor risk: Microsoft already logs AI interactions for eDiscovery and compliance. Its audit records hold references and metadata, not a breach-notification analysis.

competitors.name: Relativity (Data Breach Response, claiR)
competitors.what_they_do: Breach-response review workflow with AI-based PII detection, used by law firms and IR vendors to build notification lists. The fetch showed no support for generative-AI chat exports as a data source. Any breach-review vendor could add ChatGPT export ingestion as a connector, which would reduce the moat.

white_space:
Across the pages I could fetch, no vendor sells the specific deliverable: a counsel-facing 'what could the attacker have read, and does notification trigger' determination for a stolen AI session. The gap sits between three groups. Infostealer-intel vendors (Hudson Rock, SpyCloud, Flare, Constella) detect the stolen session but stop there. AI-DLP and DSPM vendors (Varonis, Cyera, Harmonic, Cyberhaven, Reco, Purview) classify current or real-time chat data for the customer's own governance. Breach-review platforms (Relativity and IR firms) build notification lists but show no ingestion of AI chat transcripts. What remains open is the forensic and legal bridge: joining the theft window from the feed with provider-side session-access evidence and the chat content, then producing a privilege-friendly memo and affected-person list.

Caveats on the wedge:
- The WebSearch budget ran out, so I could not check funded startups, Product Hunt, YC or open-source projects. A stealth startup is possible.
- I could not verify the '358 of 482' or '80,000 domains' figures.
- The wedge depends on data access. A theft of a personal or free-tier account leaves the employer with no export. Only Enterprise and Edu tenants have admin export or Compliance API data, and I could not confirm the current API terms because the OpenAI help pages returned 403.
- A stolen cookie in a feed does not prove the attacker viewed the chats, so the assessment depends on provider audit logs that only OpenAI or the tenant admin can see.
- Any vendor holding the customer's chat data (Cyera, Varonis, Purview) can add this as a services line quickly.
evidence_of_demand:
No direct evidence found that breach counsel or insurers currently pay for AI-chat-history exposure assessments. I found no RFPs, forum complaints or published incident cases. Indirect signals are limited to the following:
- Exposure is real. Group-IB found 101,134 stealer-infected devices with saved ChatGPT credentials (https://www.group-ib.com/media-center/press-releases/stealers-chatgpt-credentials/).
- Vendors are building and selling AI-chat governance, which shows enterprise budget for the adjacent problem. Varonis markets ChatGPT Enterprise data protection (https://www.varonis.com/products/ai-security). Harmonic markets prompt classification (https://www.harmonic.security/). Cyera markets AI Prompt Security and an 'Incident Materiality Assessment' (https://www.cyera.com/). Reco has raised $85M in total (https://www.reco.ai/).
- Microsoft charges pay-as-you-go for audit logs of non-Microsoft AI apps, with 180-day retention, so a compliance and eDiscovery market for AI interactions is forming (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/purview/audit-copilot).
- Relativity sells a Data Breach Response product (https://www.relativity.com/data-solutions/), so there is a paid breach-notification review workflow, but I found no AI-chat support in it.

I could not verify the idea's claims about insurer AI exclusions or the incident statistics.
sharper_angle:
Narrow the offer to a provider-evidence scoping service, sold as a white-label module rather than a standalone brand.

1. Sell only where a defensible answer exists: ChatGPT Enterprise and Edu tenants, and other enterprise AI tenants with admin audit or Compliance API logs. The product is a 48-hour determination of whether the stolen session was actually used (provider session, IP and device logs against the infostealer theft window) and what chat content sat in scope. The main value is defensible non-notification. Counsel and insurers pay to avoid over-notifying, and the incumbents' classification tools cannot make that call because they lack the theft-window evidence.
2. Do not build a broad classification platform. Ship a connector and a rules pack. It ingests the Compliance API export and produces review-ready PII, PHI, credential and deal-data tags inside Relativity-style breach-review workflows, so IR boutiques and data-mining vendors resell it rather than compete with it.
3. Lead with insurer panels and breach counsel under privilege (counsel-engaged, Kovel-style). A per-incident fee needs the vendor to be a trusted third party.
4. Keep a monthly retainer only for pre-incident 'AI-session readiness': retention settings, log export enabled, and a session-revocation runbook. Pre-incident readiness is the cheaper way to test demand before incident volume proves out.
5. Before building, validate with 5 to 10 breach counsel and IR leads. Ask how many AI-session-theft matters they have seen in the last 12 months. If the answer is near zero, this is a feature for Cyera or Varonis, not a company. If it is more than a handful, a per-incident business is plausible.
